clinicalPearls: Sedation exists on a continuum from minimal sedation to general anaesthesia, and patients can drift into a deeper level than intended, so providers must be able to rescue from the next deeper level
The most common serious complications are respiratory: airway obstruction, hypoventilation, apnoea, and hypoxaemia, which can progress rapidly if unrecognised
Cardiovascular effects include hypotension and bradycardia, and combining sedatives with opioids markedly increases the risk of respiratory depression
Continuous monitoring of oxygenation with pulse oximetry and of ventilation with capnography, plus regular assessment of conscious level, is essential throughout and during recovery
Appropriate patient selection and pre-procedure assessment (airway, comorbidities, aspiration risk, and fasting status) reduce complications
Resuscitation equipment, oxygen, suction, and reversal agents must be immediately available, and staff must be trained to manage airway and cardiovascular emergencies
Reversal agents (such as an opioid antagonist for opioids and a benzodiazepine antagonist for benzodiazepines) can be used, but their duration may be shorter than the sedative, risking re-sedation
Elderly, frail, obese, and sleep-apnoea patients, and those at the extremes of age, are especially vulnerable and warrant conservative dosing and heightened vigilance
reference.pathophysiology: Sedative and analgesic agents depress the central nervous system in a dose-dependent way, reducing conscious level, blunting protective airway reflexes, and depressing respiratory drive and upper airway muscle tone. Loss of pharyngeal tone causes obstruction, while reduced central drive causes hypoventilation and apnoea, together producing hypoxaemia and hypercapnia. Many agents also cause vasodilation and myocardial depression, leading to hypotension, and some blunt compensatory reflexes. Because effects are additive, combinations of sedatives and opioids produce disproportionate respiratory and cardiovascular depression. Depressed reflexes also raise the risk of aspiration in patients with a full stomach.
additionalDifferentials: Underlying cardiac or respiratory disease causing deterioration
Hypoglycaemia or metabolic disturbance altering consciousness
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity when combined with local blocks
additionalInvestigations: Continuous pulse oximetry and capnography during sedation and recovery
Regular assessment of sedation depth and responsiveness
Blood pressure and ECG monitoring appropriate to patient risk
Arterial or capillary blood gas if significant hypoventilation is suspected
Glucose check if altered consciousness is unexplained
redFlags: Apnoea, severe hypoventilation, or airway obstruction with falling oxygen saturation
Unintended progression to deep sedation or general anaesthesia without rescue capability
Aspiration during sedation in an at-risk patient
reference.prognosis: With appropriate patient selection, monitoring, and prompt rescue, procedural sedation is generally safe; unrecognised respiratory depression can cause hypoxic injury or death, and most serious events are linked to inadequate monitoring or rescue.
pitfalls: Providing sedation without the skills or equipment to rescue a deeper-than-intended level
Relying on oximetry alone and missing early hypoventilation that capnography would detect
Underestimating the additive respiratory depression of sedative-opioid combinations
Assuming a reversal agent fully solves the problem despite its shorter duration and risk of re-sedation
Inadequate pre-procedure assessment of airway, comorbidity, and aspiration risk
management: Prevent complications through pre-procedure assessment of airway, comorbidity, aspiration risk and fasting status, with appropriate patient selection
Monitor oxygenation with pulse oximetry and ventilation with capnography, and assess conscious level throughout the procedure and recovery
Manage respiratory depression with supplemental oxygen, airway-opening manoeuvres, airway adjuncts and assisted ventilation
Administer reversal agents where appropriate, naloxone for opioids and flumazenil for benzodiazepines
Support the circulation with intravenous fluids and vasopressors for hypotension and an antimuscarinic such as atropine for bradycardia
Ensure immediate availability of oxygen, suction and resuscitation and airway equipment, with staff trained to rescue from a deeper-than-intended level of sedation
Escalate to anaesthetic and critical care support for failure to rescue or aspiration
